progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: pathogen, host, the groups (bacteria, fungi, protozoa, helminths, viruses) and their plant cases: crown gall (bacterium), wheat stem rust (fungus), root-knot nematodes (helminth), tobacco mosaic virus. From b03: modes of transmission, fomites (contaminated objects) and that control must match the route. From bio-m5-b01: the Cavendish banana is a clone, so plantations share one weakness to disease. From bio-m5-b03b: copying a winner gives a uniform crop with a shared weakness; selective breeding and artificial pollination for rust resistance in wheat. From Year 11: leaves photosynthesise; xylem carries water up from roots. Not assumed: the three things a disease needs, direct against indirect effects, export dependence, how to assess an effect, myrtle rust, foot-and-mouth disease.
progression.startsWith: Compare plant and animal cases. The video opens: In April 2010, a rust fungus turned up on plants at one nursery on the New South Wales Central Coast.
progression.stopsAfter: stating the three things disease needs (pathogen, a host it can infect, the right conditions); explaining how a paddock of one variety and the movement of plants and soil raise the risk; describing direct effects on crops (yield, quality, control costs) with mechanisms for rust and nematodes; assessing myrtle rust (cause: an introduced rust fungus meeting myrtles with little resistance, spread by wind and nursery plants; effects on lemon myrtle and tea tree plantations, on native species, and permanence); describing foot-and-mouth disease (virus, cloven-hoofed animals, spread, blisters, reduced milk and meat, low adult death rate); separating direct effects (in the sick animals) from indirect effects (control and closed markets) with the 2001 United Kingdom outbreak; explaining why indirect effects usually dominate for an exporter like Australia; assessing an effect by size, duration and reach; distinguishing direct and indirect effects in an unseen outbreak and giving biological and agricultural causes of crop losses.
progression.nextLesson: how a named Australian plant defends itself against a named pathogen: a banksia against *Phytophthora cinnamomi* (route entry bio-m7-b05).

teaching.task: How does disease damage farm production, and why does the bill so often reach far past the sick plants and animals?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why wet weather matters (spores need water to germinate; scene 2); why one variety raises losses (every plant equally susceptible, nothing slows spread; scene 3); how rust and nematodes cut yield (sugars and leaf area; squeezed xylem; scene 4); why Australian myrtles were hit hard (no shared history, little resistance, not "foreign"; scene 5); why myrtle rust costs are permanent (cannot be eradicated; scene 6); why most culled animals were healthy (whole herds on infected and neighbouring farms, plus welfare culls of stock stranded by movement bans; scene 8); why exporters suffer most (most beef sold overseas; one case closes markets; scene 9). Visible case: the spread map, the leaf pair crossfade, the hoof pair crossfade, chips moving across the gate line, the cost bars. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; scene 8 is the densest (the dot grid plus three chips), so the dot grid stays grey except the amber few.
teaching.conversationalApproach: In April 2010 a rust fungus turned up at one nursery on the New South Wales Central Coast and within a few years had spread the length of the east coast, so the question is how disease damages farm production and why the bill so often reaches far past the sick plants and animals. Causes come first: a pathogen, a host it can infect and the right conditions have to meet, and farming tips the odds because a paddock of one variety shares one weakness (the Cavendish banana recalled) and moving plants, soil and machinery carries pathogens. A crop's costs are traced as yield, quality and control cost, with rust pustules taking sugars and nematode galls squeezing the xylem. Myrtle rust is the plant case (an overseas fungus meeting myrtles with little resistance, wind and nursery spread, fungicide costs in dense plantations, an endangered native guava and no eradication), and foot-and-mouth disease is the animal case, separating direct effects in sick animals from the indirect costs of Britain's 2001 culls, closed markets and tourism losses, and showing why an exporter like Australia fears the indirect effects most. An effect is assessed by how big, how long and how far, and the memory aid is count past the farm gate. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In April 2010, a rust fungus turned up on plants at one nursery on the New South Wales Central Coast. Within a few years it had spread the length of the east coast, on eucalypts, paperbarks and lemon myrtle. So how does disease damage farm production, and why does the bill so often reach far past the sick plants and animals?
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a distinguishes direct from indirect effects of a hypothetical foot-and-mouth outbreak in an exporting country and asks which costs more (the route's stop: production losses and control consequences). 12c asks for one biological and one agricultural cause of district-wide rust losses (the "causes" half of the dotpoint, and the scene 3 idea). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reason, givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B7-IQ1-03: "assess the causes and effects of diseases on agricultural production, including but not limited to:", with its listed examples "plant diseases" and "animal diseases". Verb "assess" (make a judgement of value, quality, outcomes, results or size): scene 10 gives the criteria, scenes 6, 8 and 9 apply them, and both attempts ask for judged causes or effects rather than lists.

design.visualSystem: One farm gate ledger board: a coded vertical dashed line down the right third of the frame, labelled in small grey handwriting "farm gate", splits the board into "on the farm" (left) and "past the farm gate" (right). A cause strip sits along the top left (scene 2's three parts). Effect chips land on the side where the cost falls: yield, quality and sick animals on the left (teal tag "direct"); culled healthy herds, movement bans, closed exports, tourism and ecosystems on the right (amber tag "indirect" or green tag "beyond the farm"). Painted plates carry each case: diseased against healthy plates appear as aligned pairs that crossfade (the myrtle leaf pair, the hoof pair); the wheat rust plate is already a side-by-side pair. No people, hands, faces or farmers: farms are shown by crops, animals, a gate, a stock truck and a shipping container. Coded elements are abstract only: the gate line, chips, arrows, a small coded map outline of Australia for the spread (scene 6), a dotted spread path, and cost bars in scene 8. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides small grey labels; earlier chips dim to grey when the next lands. Plates are scaled proportionally, never stretched.
